title: Clinical Features And Tests For Malabsorption

questions.q: The first step in evaluating malabsorption is to:
questions.exp: Steps for evaluating malabsorption: 1. confirm the diagnosis (clinically / by investigations). (Book p14)

questions.q: Order the printed steps — 1) Step 1 2) Step 2 3) Step 3 … A) Confirm global vs selective malabsorption B) Confirm the diagnosis C) Confirm the aetiology
questions.exp: 1. Confirm the diagnosis, 2. confirm global vs selective malabsorption, 3. confirm the aetiology. (Book p14)

questions.q: The second step after confirming the diagnosis of malabsorption is to:
questions.exp: 2. Confirm global vs selective malabsorption. (Book p14)

questions.q: The final step in the book's evaluation sequence is to:
questions.exp: 3. Confirm the aetiology. (Book p14)

questions.q: The diagnosis of malabsorption is confirmed clinically and by ____.
questions.exp: Step 1: confirm the diagnosis — clinically and by investigations. (Book p14)

questions.q: In the clinical features table, the diarrhoea of malabsorption arises from which site?
questions.exp: Clinical features — diarrhoea: site — small intestine. (Book p14)

questions.q: The duration of diarrhoea in the malabsorption table is:
questions.exp: Clinical features — duration: >4 weeks. (Book p14)

questions.q: The stool osmotic gap in malabsorption is:
questions.exp: Clinical features: stool osmotic gap ↑. (Book p14)

questions.q: The diarrhoea of malabsorption is described as ____ diarrhoea and is the most consistent symptom.
questions.exp: Osmotic diarrhoea: most consistent symptom. (Book p14)

questions.q: On fasting, the diarrhoea of malabsorption:
questions.exp: Clinical features: improves on fasting. (Book p14)

questions.q: Gastrointestinal — fat malabsorption presents as:
opts: Foul smelling stools, ascites and edema
questions.exp: Gastrointestinal: fat malabsorption → steatorrhea. (Book p14)

questions.q: Gastrointestinal — carbohydrate malabsorption presents as:
opts: Foul smelling stools, ascites and edema
questions.exp: Gastrointestinal: carbohydrate malabsorption → abdominal bloating and dyspeptic symptoms. (Book p14)

questions.q: Gastrointestinal — protein malabsorption presents as:
opts: Foul smelling stools, ascites and edema
questions.exp: Gastrointestinal: protein malabsorption → foul smelling stools, ascites, edema. (Book p14)

questions.q: Match the macronutrient malabsorbed to the printed gut feature — 1) Fat 2) Carbohydrate 3) Protein … A) Foul smelling stools, ascites, edema B) Steatorrhea C) Abdominal bloating and dyspeptic symptoms
questions.exp: Fat → steatorrhea; carbohydrate → abdominal bloating and dyspeptic symptoms; protein → foul smelling stools, ascites, edema. (Book p14)

questions.q: The fourth gastrointestinal feature listed is:
questions.exp: Gastrointestinal: unexplained weight loss. (Book p14)

questions.q: Musculoskeletal features of malabsorption are attributed to:
opts: Fat malabsorption due to impaired vitamin D and calcium absorption
questions.exp: Musculoskeletal: fat malabsorption d/t impaired vitamin D and Ca2+ absorption. (Book p14)

questions.q: The musculoskeletal features listed are:
questions.exp: Musculoskeletal: tetany, fracture, bone pain. (Book p14)

questions.q: Cutaneous — hyperpigmentation is attributed to deficiency of:
questions.exp: Cutaneous manifestations: vitamin B3 / niacin deficiency → hyperpigmentation. (Book p14)

questions.q: Cutaneous — perifollicular hemorrhage and curly (spiral) hair indicate deficiency of:
questions.exp: Cutaneous: vitamin C deficiency → perifollicular hemorrhage, curly hair / spiral hair. (Book p14)

questions.q: Cutaneous — bruisability and ecchymoses indicate deficiency of:
questions.exp: Cutaneous: vitamin K deficiency → bruisability, ecchymoses. (Book p14)

questions.q: Cutaneous — acrodermatitis is attributed to deficiency of:
questions.exp: Cutaneous: Zn / essential fatty acid deficiency → acrodermatitis. (Book p14)

questions.q: Cutaneous — follicular hyperkeratosis indicates deficiency of:
questions.exp: Cutaneous: vitamin A deficiency → follicular hyperkeratosis. (Book p14)

questions.q: Match the cutaneous sign to the printed deficiency — 1) Hyperpigmentation 2) Perifollicular hemorrhage, curly hair 3) Bruisability, ecchymoses 4) Acrodermatitis … A) Vitamin K B) Niacin (B3) C) Zinc / essential fatty acids D) Vitamin C
questions.exp: Niacin → hyperpigmentation; vitamin C → perifollicular hemorrhage and curly hair; vitamin K → bruisability/ecchymoses; Zn and essential fatty acids → acrodermatitis. (Book p14)

questions.q: Miscellaneous — coeliac disease in the table presents with:
questions.exp: Miscellaneous: coeliac disease → growth retardation. (Book p14)

questions.q: Anaemia due to intestinal malabsorption — distal pathology produces:
questions.exp: Anaemia (d/t intestinal malabsorption): distal pathology → vitamin B12 deficiency. (Book p14)

questions.q: Anaemia due to intestinal malabsorption — proximal pathology produces:
questions.exp: Anaemia: proximal pathology → folate / iron deficiency. (Book p14)

questions.q: Match the level of intestinal pathology to the printed anaemia — 1) Proximal 2) Distal … A) Vitamin B12 deficiency B) Folate / iron deficiency
questions.exp: Proximal pathology → folate / iron deficiency; distal pathology → vitamin B12 deficiency. (Book p14)

questions.q: Peripheral neuropathy and ataxia in the miscellaneous column are attributed to:
questions.exp: Miscellaneous: vitamin B12 / E deficiency → peripheral neuropathy, ataxia. (Book p14)

questions.q: Glossitis, cheliosis and stomatitis are attributed to:
questions.exp: Miscellaneous: vitamin B12 deficiency → glossitis, cheliosis, stomatitis. (Book p14)

questions.q: Night blindness and xerophthalmia are attributed to:
questions.exp: Miscellaneous: vitamin A deficiency → night blindness, xerophthalmia. (Book p14)

questions.q: Pick the ODD ONE OUT — one of these is not a listed miscellaneous feature of malabsorption:
questions.exp: Miscellaneous lists growth retardation, anaemia, peripheral neuropathy/ataxia, glossitis-cheliosis-stomatitis and night blindness. Arthralgia is not listed. (Book p14)

questions.q: In normal physiology, fatty acid binds calcium to form an ____ that is excreted.
questions.exp: Normal physiology: fatty acid + Ca2+ → insoluble → excreted. (Book p15)

questions.q: In malabsorption, unbound oxalate in the gut is:
opts: Absorbed in the colon producing oxaluria
Metabolised by colonic bacteria to lactate
questions.exp: In malabsorption: free oxalate in gut → oxalate absorbed in colon → oxaluria. (Book p15)

questions.q: Order the printed kidney stone pathway — 1) Free oxalate in gut 2) Oxalate absorbed in colon 3) Oxaluria 4) Ca2+ oxalate stones … A) Oxaluria B) Free oxalate in gut C) Ca2+ oxalate stones D) Oxalate absorbed in colon
questions.exp: Free oxalate in gut → oxalate absorbed in colon → oxaluria → Ca2+ oxalate stones. (Book p15)

questions.q: The kidney stones of malabsorption are composed of:
questions.exp: Malabsorption → Ca2+ oxalate stones in urine. (Book p15)

questions.q: All of the following are listed as NOT seen in malabsorption EXCEPT:
questions.exp: Note: symptoms not seen in malabsorption — abdominal pain, constipation, fever. Steatorrhea is a feature. (Book p15)

questions.q: The note lists symptoms that are not seen in malabsorption as:
questions.exp: Note: symptoms not seen in malabsorption — abdominal pain, constipation, fever. (Book p15)

questions.q: Match the differential of malabsorption to the printed similarity — 1) TB 2) Nephrotic syndrome … A) Protein loss B) Weight loss, long standing diarrhoea, edema/ascites
questions.exp: Differentials of malabsorption (similar symptoms): TB — weight loss, long standing diarrhoea, edema/ascites; nephrotic syndrome — protein loss. (Book p15)

questions.q: A patient has chronic diarrhoea, weight loss and ascites. Before calling it malabsorption the book asks you to exclude:
questions.exp: Differentials of malabsorption with similar symptoms: TB — weight loss, long standing diarrhoea, edema/ascites. (Book p15)

questions.q: The qualitative test for fat malabsorption listed is:
questions.exp: Fat malabsorption: qualitative test — Sudan III. (Book p15)

questions.q: The quantitative test for fat malabsorption is:
questions.exp: Quantitative test (gold standard): fecal fat excretion >7 g/day. (Book p15)

questions.q: The quantitative fecal fat test is abnormal above:
questions.exp: Quantitative test (gold standard): fecal fat excretion >7 g/day. (Book p15)

questions.q: The book calls the fecal fat excretion test:
opts: The gold standard investigation for malabsorption
A test of pancreatic function only
questions.exp: Note: fecal fat excretion test is the gold standard investigation for malabsorption. (Book p15)

questions.q: TRUE or FALSE — Sudan III is listed as the qualitative stool fat test in this chapter's investigations.
opts: False — Oil red O is the only listed stain
True — but it is the gold standard
questions.exp: Fat malabsorption: qualitative test — Sudan III; quantitative test (gold standard) — fecal fat excretion >7 g/day. (Book p15)

questions.q: The D-xylose test is described as:
opts: The best and most specific test for carbohydrate malabsorption
The gold standard for fat malabsorption
A test of pancreatic exocrine function
An obsolete test of bile acid absorption
questions.exp: Carbohydrate malabsorption: 1. D-xylose test — best and most specific test. (Book p15)

questions.q: D-xylose is composed of:
opts: A disaccharide of glucose and galactose
questions.exp: Composition of D-xylose: pentose monosaccharide. (Book p15)

questions.q: The D-xylose test is used to assess:
questions.exp: Used to assess intact small intestinal mucosa (D-xylose absorbed here). (Book p15)

questions.q: The dose of D-xylose given orally after fasting is:
questions.exp: Procedure: 25 g of D-xylose given orally after fasting (early morning). (Book p15)

questions.q: After the oral dose, urine is collected for how long?
questions.exp: Collect urine sample (entire volume passed) after 4-6 hours and check D-xylose levels. (Book p15)

questions.q: A normal D-xylose excretion result is:
questions.exp: Interpretation: normal ≥4.5 g. (Book p15)

questions.q: A positive (abnormal) D-xylose test is reported below:
questions.exp: <4.5 g (positive) → small intestinal mucosal pathology. (Book p15)

questions.q: A positive D-xylose test indicates ____ pathology.
questions.exp: <4.5 g (positive) → small intestinal mucosal pathology. (Book p15)

questions.q: Match the clinical scenario to the printed reason for a false positive D-xylose — 1) Renal failure 2) Rapid intestinal transit 3) SIBO 4) Ascites … A) Reduced absorption B) Defective excretion C) Organisms utilise D-xylose → reduced absorption D) Reduced absorption
questions.exp: Renal failure → defective excretion; rapid intestinal transit (hyperthyroidism, vomiting) → reduced absorption; SIBO → organisms utilise D-xylose → reduced absorption; ascites → reduced absorption. (Book p16)

questions.q: Renal failure causes a false positive D-xylose test because of:
questions.exp: Renal failure: defective excretion → false positive. (Book p16)

questions.q: Rapid intestinal transit causing a false positive D-xylose is listed with:
questions.exp: Rapid intestinal transit (hyperthyroidism, vomiting) → reduced absorption → false positive. (Book p16)

questions.q: SIBO produces a false positive D-xylose test because:
opts: Organisms utilise D-xylose, so absorption is reduced
questions.exp: SIBO: organisms utilise D-xylose → reduced absorption → false positive. (Book p16)

questions.q: The lactose tolerance test is described as:
questions.exp: 2. Lactose tolerance test: obsolete. (Book p16)

questions.q: The lactose hydrogen breath test is done for:
questions.exp: 3. Lactose H2 breath test: done for lactase deficiency. (Book p16)

questions.q: Order the printed principle of the lactose H2 breath test — 1) Deficiency of lactase 2) Accumulation of lactose in large intestine 3) Bacterial action on lactose 4) H2 production … A) H2 production B) Deficiency of lactase C) Bacterial action on lactose D) Accumulation of lactose in large intestine
questions.exp: Deficiency of lactase → accumulation of lactose in large intestine → bacterial action on lactose → H2 production. (Book p16)

questions.q: Diagnosis on the lactose hydrogen breath test is a rise in breath H2 of:
questions.exp: Diagnosis: ↑ in breath H2 > 20 ppm. (Book p16)

questions.q: The lactulose H2 breath test is used to detect:
opts: Bacterial overgrowth of the small intestine
questions.exp: 4. Lactulose H2 breath test: H2 produced within 90 minutes (early peaking) = SIBO. (Book p16)

questions.q: On the lactulose H2 breath test, an early peak of H2 within what time indicates SIBO?
questions.exp: H2 produced within 90 minutes (early peaking) → SIBO. (Book p16)

questions.q: On the lactulose H2 breath test, H2 appearing after 90 minutes indicates:
questions.exp: >90 minutes = normal physiology. (Book p16)

questions.q: Match the obsolete test to the printed malabsorption it was used for — 1) Acid steatocrit test 2) C-14 triolein breath test 3) C-13 egg white breath test … A) Protein malabsorption B) Fat malabsorption C) Fat malabsorption
questions.exp: Obsolete tests: acid steatocrit test and C-14 triolein breath test for fat malabsorption; C-13 egg white breath test (phenol and p-cresol in urine) for protein malabsorption. (Book p16)

questions.q: The acid steatocrit test was an obsolete test for:
questions.exp: Obsolete tests for malabsorption: acid steatocrit test — fat malabsorption. (Book p16)

questions.q: The C-14 triolein breath test was an obsolete test for:
questions.exp: Obsolete: C-14 triolein breath test — fat malabsorption. (Book p16)

questions.q: The C-13 egg white breath test detects protein malabsorption by measuring:
questions.exp: C-13 egg white breath test (phenol and p-cresol in urine) — protein malabsorption. (Book p16)

questions.q: Stool elastase and chymotrypsin are noted as tests for:
questions.exp: Note: stool elastase, chymotrypsin — pancreatic insufficiency. (Book p16)

questions.q: Fecal α-1 antitrypsin is the noted test for:
questions.exp: Note: fecal α-1 antitrypsin — primary intestinal lymphangiectasia. (Book p16)

questions.q: NIRA (near infrared reflectance analysis) is described as:
opts: An obsolete test for fat malabsorption
A test of ileal bile acid transport
questions.exp: Note: NIRA (near infrared reflectance analysis) — newer test for malabsorption. (Book p16)

questions.q: The diseases the book says are diagnosed on biopsy are:
opts: Coeliac disease, tropical sprue and SIBO
questions.exp: Diseases diagnosed on biopsy: 1. Whipple's disease, 2. agammaglobulinaemia, 3. abetalipoproteinaemia. (Book p16)

questions.q: Phase I of the Schilling test begins with unlabelled vitamin B12 given:
questions.exp: Phase I: 1000 μg of unlabelled vitamin B12 I.M. to saturate stores. (Book p17)

questions.q: The dose of oral radiolabelled vitamin B12 in the Schilling test is:
questions.exp: Give 1 μg of oral radiolabelled vitamin B12. (Book p17)

questions.q: After the doses, the Schilling test measures vitamin B12 in:
questions.exp: Check vitamin B12 level in urine. (Book p17)

questions.q: A urinary vitamin B12 excretion below what value is a positive Schilling test?
questions.exp: <7% = positive test (malabsorption aetiology). (Book p17)

questions.q: Urinary vitamin B12 excretion of 7-10% in the Schilling test is:
questions.exp: 7-10% = normal. (Book p17)

questions.q: Match phase II of the Schilling test to the diagnosis when urine B12 rises above 10% — 1) Intrinsic factor 2) Pancreatic enzymes 3) Antibiotics … A) Chronic pancreatitis B) SIBO C) Pernicious anaemia
questions.exp: Phase II: administer intrinsic factor / pancreatic enzymes / antibiotics; if urine B12 >10% → pernicious anaemia (IF), chronic pancreatitis, SIBO respectively. (Book p17)

questions.q: After phase I and II, persistent urine B12 below 7% indicates:
questions.exp: After phase I and II, if urine B12 <7% = ileal disease. (Book p17)

questions.q: A patient's Schilling test corrects after oral intrinsic factor is added in phase II. The book's diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Phase II: intrinsic factor → urine B12 >10% → pernicious anaemia (IF). (Book p17)

questions.q: A patient's Schilling test corrects after antibiotics in phase II. The book's diagnosis is:
questions.exp: Phase II: antibiotics → urine B12 >10% → SIBO. (Book p17)

units.title: Steps for Evaluating Malabsorption
units.guide:
Confirm the diagnosis (clinically and by investigations).
Then confirm global versus selective malabsorption.
Finally confirm the aetiology.

units.title: Clinical Features: Gastrointestinal
units.guide:
Small intestinal, >4 weeks, osmotic, improves on fasting — the most consistent symptom.
Fat → steatorrhea; carbohydrate → bloating and dyspepsia.
Protein → foul smelling stools, ascites, edema; plus unexplained weight loss.

units.title: Clinical Features: Musculoskeletal & Cutaneous
units.guide:
Musculoskeletal: fat malabsorption with impaired vitamin D and Ca2+ → tetany, fracture, bone pain.
Niacin → hyperpigmentation; vitamin C → perifollicular hemorrhage and curly hair.
Vitamin K → bruisability; Zn/EFA → acrodermatitis; vitamin A → follicular hyperkeratosis.

units.title: Clinical Features: Miscellaneous & Kidney Stones
units.guide:
Coeliac → growth retardation; proximal disease → folate/iron deficiency; distal → B12 deficiency.
B12/E → neuropathy and ataxia; B12 → glossitis, cheliosis, stomatitis; vitamin A → night blindness.
Free oxalate is absorbed in the colon → oxaluria → Ca2+ oxalate stones; pain, constipation and fever are NOT features.

units.title: Fat Malabsorption Tests
units.guide:
Qualitative: Sudan III.
Quantitative (gold standard): fecal fat excretion >7 g/day.
The fecal fat excretion test is the gold standard investigation for malabsorption.

units.title: D-Xylose Test
units.guide:
Best and most specific test; D-xylose is a pentose monosaccharide.
It assesses intact small intestinal mucosa.
25 g orally after fasting; urine collected over 4-6 hours; normal ≥4.5 g, <4.5 g positive.

units.title: False Positives & Hydrogen Breath Tests
units.guide:
False positives: renal failure (defective excretion), rapid transit (hyperthyroidism, vomiting), SIBO (organisms utilise D-xylose), ascites.
Lactose H2 breath test: for lactase deficiency, positive >20 ppm.
Lactulose H2 breath test: H2 within 90 minutes = SIBO; after 90 minutes = normal.

units.title: Obsolete Tests & Biopsy Diagnoses
units.guide:
Obsolete: acid steatocrit and C-14 triolein breath test (fat); C-13 egg white breath test (protein).
Stool elastase/chymotrypsin → pancreatic insufficiency; fecal α-1 antitrypsin → lymphangiectasia; NIRA is newer.
Biopsy diagnoses: Whipple's disease, agammaglobulinaemia, abetalipoproteinaemia.

units.title: Schilling Test
units.guide:
Phase I: 1000 μg unlabelled B12 IM to saturate stores, then 1 μg oral radiolabelled B12, then urine B12.
<7% positive, 7-10% normal.
Phase II: intrinsic factor → pernicious anaemia; pancreatic enzymes → chronic pancreatitis; antibiotics → SIBO; still <7% = ileal disease.
